analysis.one_liner: Requires the FDA to pull one approved opioid painkiller off the market for every new one it approves.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with zero cosponsors and never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced the Food and Drug Administration to revoke the approval of one already-approved opioid pain medication each time it approved a new one, with instructions to prioritize pulling the most dangerous, non-abuse-deterrent pills. Its stated aim was to shrink the oversupply of prescription opioids behind tens of thousands of overdose deaths a year.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to prescription opioids — patients, families, and communities hit by the overdose epidemic — would gain if the supply of dangerous pain pills on the market were reduced one-for-one as new ones enter.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities hit by the opioid epidemic

how_it_helps.text: For every new opioid painkiller the FDA approves, the agency must revoke approval of an existing one, shrinking the total number of opioid products on the market.
The FDA must prioritize revoking approval of opioids that are not abuse-deterrent, and weigh the public health impact of each drug before choosing which to pull.

The bill's findings cite more than 33,000 opioid overdose deaths in 2015, with nearly half involving prescription opioids, and note the U.S. consumes 80 percent of the world's opioid pain medications.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical companies that make opioid pain medications would lose an approved product each time a new one is approved, cutting into a market worth billions a year. Some chronic pain patients could face a smaller menu of pain treatment options as products are pulled.

drawbacks.text: The one-for-one rule is rigid: a genuinely safer, harder-to-abuse new painkiller could only enter the market by displacing another drug, with no flexibility for FDA judgment about whether the swap actually helps public health.
Pulling opioid products off the market could squeeze patients with chronic pain who rely on prescription opioids, a concern that shaped the broader opioid policy debate during this Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill attacked a documented public health catastrophe — an opioid oversupply that had quadrupled since 1999 — with a simple, automatic mechanism. Its strength was that it required no annual congressional action and targeted the most dangerous formulations first. Its weakness was bluntness: a fixed one-in-one-out quota lets no room for FDA medical judgment, and patients with serious pain could have lost treatment options. A more flexible version might have achieved the same goal with fewer collateral risks.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to the Health Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Joe Manchin introduced the bill on May 9, 2017, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill never reached the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opioid painkiller manufacturers, who kept every approved product on the market and faced no requirement to cede shelf space to new competitors. The bill's death also meant the FDA faced no new mandate to remove dangerous formulations.

for.name: Sen. Joe Manchin III
for.role: U.S. Senator from West Virginia; bill's sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave it its only Senate action; it died in committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress; it never got a hearing or a vote.

against.name: Opioid painkiller manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Continued marketing and defending a product category that the bill would have forced to shrink; the industry was broadly resisting restrictions on opioid prescribing during this period.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no other senator cosponsored the bill, so there is no record of where either party stood beyond one Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: The bill would have taken one approved opioid product off the market for every new one approved, directly shrinking the size of their market. The industry's interest in keeping products on shelves ran against the bill's goal of reducing overdose deaths.
Only opioid painkillers were targeted; the bill's mechanism applied to a single drug class under FDA approval authority, leaving the broader industry untouched.
